The refusal is immediate, and the voices divide over who led it. Gill takes Azariah for Jezaniah or a brother of his, named first because the scheme was his; two versions, he notes, give him a different father. Ellicott sees the same name-swap between Greek and Hebrew, allows that the names may be brothers who both led, and reads the precedence over Johanan as marking him chief spokesman. Calvin declines the question — of Azariah nothing certain can be known — and turns to Johanan, whom he had earlier taken for a heroic man, bold and prudent and upright, and who now heads the rebellion.

What they say is a flat denial. Clarke observes they had no other colour for rebellion than to deny outright that God had spoken. Henry finds the cause under the colour: it was pride, and only by pride comes contention with God and man; the proud unhumbled heart is one of the most daring enemies God has on this side hell. Ellicott reads the naming of the proud men as implying that others, left to themselves, would have followed the prophet, and adds that the Greek follows a different Hebrew and gives all the aliens where the English has all the proud.

The charge against Baruch is where they part company. Gill calls it unlikely on its face — the prophet was not to be prevailed on by a younger man who was his own secretary, Baruch had no interest to serve, and both were too good men for it. Calvin makes it a fallback: finding no reason to say Jeremiah lied, they turned their fury on a man as innocent, charging him with wanting to betray them to slaughter. Ellicott alone allows the suspicion some colour, pointing to a later warning that suggests a certain ambition in Baruch, noting he would have been known as advocating submission, and recording that an apocryphal book places him at Babylon when the city fell.

Then the whole company goes. Calvin presses that the guilt is general, not the captains' only: they had asked what God's will was and rose against the prophet when it did not suit them, and the people are brought in with the leaders so none should think it strange that innocent men went into Egypt with them. He also explains where the returned remnant came from: fugitives among the Moabites and Edomites who came back once Gedaliah had leave to gather them.

That the king's daughters were there at all surprises Clarke, who offers three reasons why the Chaldeans might have left any of the royal house: they may not have known of them; or thought children of concubines could not inherit; or held females ineligible — and they had made sure of Zedekiah's sons before their father's eyes. Calvin agrees they were probably daughters by concubines, put somewhere safe against disaster and returning with the other exiles only to be carried into Egypt. Gill differs, taking the men, women and children not as the remnant already named but as a further group out of other countries.

Where they stopped is disputed, and why. Clarke puts Tahpanhes at the extremity of Lower Egypt near Heliopolis, gives its Greek name, and thinks they halted to get the king's leave to go further in. Wesley makes it the king's residence then, which answers the same reason. Ellicott places it on the north-eastern frontier near Pelusium, sixteen Roman miles off by the old road-book, sets it beside Thebes and Memphis, connects its name with an Egyptian queen, and thinks the emigrants meant to settle. Calvin observes only that the city's name perished with its wealth, barely found in the heathen writers, and was forsaken by degrees. Clarke closes with the tradition Jerome reports: here the people Jeremiah had watched and prayed and suffered for stoned him to death, and he sealed his mission with his blood.
8:
The word finds him in Egypt, and two voices make that the point. Henry observes that when God's ministers are bound the word of the LORD is not: Jeremiah went by constraint, not choice, and God did not withdraw his favour. Calvin puts the compulsion more strongly, that he was drawn as though in chains and would sooner have died of famine in Judah, then turns it round: nothing happens but by God's purpose, so God ordered the descent, wanting his herald in Egypt.

What he is to bury the stones in is disputed. Calvin takes the place at face value, a kiln where bricks were burnt or made, near the palace gate; Gill attends to the stones, as large as he could carry in both hands. Ellicott objects that a brickkiln at a palace entrance is incongruous, and that it is hard to see why a king would set his throne on one; he reads the rare word as a brick dais before the entrance, of the kind on which a king sat to give judgment, the stones going into its mortar under a fresh coat.

He presses the same doubt into the next clause. The English takes the royal pavilion for the awning over the throne when the king sat in state; others find the leather sheet spread on the pavement, where the condemned knelt for the executioner's stroke. Taken so, the prediction is more terrible: the king sits on the buried stones not in pomp but as an avenger. Calvin's interest is elsewhere — a sign without the word is unmeaning, so the command to speak gives the stones their life.

Gill alone works the text of the next verse, where the written form gives when it cometh, it shall smite, taken with Kimchi of Nebuchadnezzar's army, against the margin the English follows, of the king himself; both, he says, are to be received. Calvin adds why the threat was needed: Egypt lay ringed by lakes and river, and the Jews thought it a quiet nest.

The shepherd's garment divides them mildly. Clarke reads it for ease: the conqueror takes the land with as little opposition and as full a confidence of ownership as a man putting on his coat. Ellicott agrees the point may be the quickness of it, and adds a suggestion found elsewhere — a shepherd so wrapping himself turns his fleecy coat inside out, so the conqueror turns the land upside down. Wesley takes the arraying of the spoils, not the land, clothing his army with what Egypt yields.

On the temples they agree that God kindles. Ellicott marks the change of person as significant, God himself firing the houses of the gods with the Chaldean for instrument, and Gill says the same, the act rightly ascribed to him though others executed it. Calvin explains why temples are named: the cruellest enemies commonly spare them, so if sanctity will not preserve these, nothing preserves a house. Clarke keeps it practical, the wooden gods burnt and the metal carried off, and Wesley has idols and people alike going captive.

Beth-shemesh they all read as Heliopolis, then differ over what stood there. Gill adds that it was the On of an older story with its priest in Joseph's day; Calvin, that heathen writers use only the Greek name; Ellicott, that the name was common wherever sun-worship prevailed, and puts it twenty miles off Memphis. On the images they part: Clarke takes them for images of the sun said to be solid gold, while Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch take them for the obelisks — Keil and Delitzsch describing two of about a hundred and fifty feet, one carried to Rome by Augustus and one thrown down in the twelfth century, Ellicott counting one granite shaft of sixty-eight feet still standing. Calvin makes it the gods of that city, chief seat of their worship.
